privacy:
The short version

chang64 can be played with no account, no sign-up and no advertising. If you wish, you can create an account to find your progress on several devices: it only takes a username and a code. Today, the site asks for neither your name nor your email address.

What is stored, and where

Your puzzle progress, your puzzle rating, your day streak and your current friend game are saved in your own browser. Without an account, they never leave it: clearing your browser data erases them, which is why the transfer code exists. With an account, a copy is kept on our server (see below).

The account (optional)

If you create an account, our server stores: your username, a fingerprint of your code and of your recovery code (the code itself never leaves your device and nobody can read it back), your progress (puzzle rating, puzzles, badges, streak, preferences, game history), the date the account was created and the date of your last activity. Nothing else: no name, no email address, no IP address.

This data is used to give you back your progress on your devices. Your username and your results (puzzle rating, puzzles solved, streak, badges, Sprint record, Elo against the computer, Elo between members) may be shown to other players in the site's leaderboards and on your player profile, along with the month your account was created. It is hosted by Cloudflare, the company that hosts the site. It is neither sold nor shared.

At any time you can download your data or delete your account from Menu, My account: deletion is immediate and final. An account left unused for two years is deleted automatically, with everything it holds; having no email address, we cannot warn you beforehand.

If you invite another member to a puzzle duel, the server also keeps that duel: both usernames, the five puzzles, and each player's score and time. It carries no message. It is deleted after 60 days, or as soon as either account is deleted.

From time to time, a logged-in player may be asked one question about the site. If you answer, the server keeps your rating from 1 to 5 and, if you write one, your comment, linked to your account. They are read only by the site's publisher, to improve chang64, are never shown to other players, and are deleted with your account.

If you ask a player to be your friend, they see your request and can accept or decline it. The server keeps the request until they answer, 60 days at most, then the list of your friends. Only you and each of your friends see that you are friends; nobody else can read the list. All of it is erased with your account.

If you look for a random opponent, the server keeps your place in the waiting room (your account, the time control and your rating) while you wait, less than a minute after your last sign of life, to pair you with the member closest to your level.

Once leagues are open, the server keeps your league, your group for the week and the number of puzzles you have solved since Monday. The players in your group see your username and that number, nothing else. This is deleted with your account.

The server also keeps the date of your last username change and, for each device where you are logged in, a fingerprint of its session key. When you change your username or delete your account, a fingerprint of the old username is kept for 30 days, so that nobody else can take it; it is then erased. If you ask to stop receiving duels from a player, it keeps that choice until you undo it or delete your account; the player is not told. The account database is located in Western Europe.

A child can create an account. Choose a username that does not let anyone recognise the child: no first name, surname, school or town.

One nuance about the network address: to stop a script from creating accounts by the hundred, each account creation is counted per connection. The server does not keep your IP address; it keeps a scrambled fingerprint of it that changes every day, from which the address cannot be read back, together with a simple counter. Both are erased the next day and are linked to no account. Wrong codes typed at login are counted in the same way (a fingerprint and a counter, erased the next day), so that someone guessing your code gets blocked without locking you out.

If you choose a country in My account, it is kept with your account and shown on your player profile; you can remove it at any time, and nothing is guessed from your connection. When two players have each added the other to their friends, each of them sees that they are friends.

If you play a live game with another member, the server holds the game while it lasts: both usernames, the moves and the clocks. It is erased about 30 minutes after the end, and an invitation left unanswered is erased after 30 minutes. A correspondence game lasts longer: it is kept for up to 14 days after it ends, and an unanswered invitation for 7 days; while the game lasts, the site also keeps who is playing, whose turn it is and the deadline for the move, so that it can show you your games in progress. The game carries no message. Only your numbers of wins, draws and losses stay with your account; they can be shown on your player profile and in the site's tables.

Measuring puzzle difficulty

When you finish or miss a puzzle, the site sends its number and a single fact: solved on the first try, or not. Nothing else goes out: no identifier, no progress, no cookie. The server only keeps two counters per puzzle (attempts and successes), with no date, no IP address and no link between two reports. They are used for one thing only: ranking puzzles by difficulty more accurately. Chang Sprint sends nothing.

Audience measurement

To know how many people visit and which pages they read, chang64 uses Cloudflare Web Analytics, run by the company that already hosts the site. It sets no cookie, does not identify you, does not follow you from one site to another and does not keep your IP address for this purpose. It records the page viewed, the site you came from, your country, the type of browser and device, and how fast the page loaded. A content blocker can switch it off without breaking anything.

Importing from Lichess

If you import games from Lichess, your browser asks lichess.org for them directly, with the username or link you typed. Lichess handles that request under its own privacy policy; nothing goes through chang64 and nothing is kept here.

Cookies

Without an account, chang64 sets no cookies. If you log in to an account, a single cookie is set: it keeps your session open on that device and is removed when you log out. It is strictly necessary for the account, is used for nothing else and follows you nowhere, so there is no consent banner to click through.

When an account is created, a second cookie notes the date on that device, for 30 days. It only serves to limit the number of accounts created from one device and holds no identifier: no account, no username, nothing about you.

Server logs

The host keeps connection logs, including IP addresses, for security and abuse prevention. Those logs fall under its own privacy policy and chang64 has no access to them.

Games played by link

A friend game lives entirely inside the link you share. The moves travel through whichever messaging app you choose; no copy is kept on this site.

A puzzle duel by link works the same way: the five puzzles, your score, your time and the username you may have typed are inside the link. Only the language and the score appear in the address our server receives, so that the link preview can show the score to beat.

Your rights

Without an account, the site collects no personal data: there is nothing to access, correct or delete. With an account, you can view and download your data, delete it along with your account, or change your code, from Menu, My account. You can also change your username there, once a week. For any other question, write to {email}. You can also contact the data protection authority of your country.

Changes

This page is updated before anything new that touches your data goes live, as it was for difficulty measurement, audience measurement and accounts. Should the site one day ask for something more (an email address for a newsletter, for example), it would be announced here first, and nothing would be switched on without your agreement.
